newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa 1976 cabinet had plan to kill protesters.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa 1976 cabinet had plan to kill protesters.

text.p: South Africa's white minority government approved plans to step up the killing of anti-apartheid demonstrators in a bid to crush black revolt 20 years ago, according to newly released cabinet minutes.

The then minister of justice and police Jimmy Kruger recommended the policy at a cabinet meeting in August 1976, the director of the state archive, Marie Olivier, said in a telephone interview on Friday.
Minutes of the meeting released on Thursday said Kruger had discussed the black student riots which broke out in Soweto township in June 1976 and rapidly spread to most other parts of the country.

"The minister proposes that this movement must be broken, and thinks the police should perhaps act more drastically and with a heavier hand, which would result in more deaths," said the minutes, written in Afrikaans and stamped "Approved".
At least 600 black demonstrators are believed to have been killed by police during several months of rioting in 1976, though some estimates put the figure higher.
The protests, originally sparked by government efforts to force blacks to use Afrikaans in school, were a major landmark in resistance to minority rule.

Thousands of black youths fled the country at the time to join exiled liberation movements such as Nelson Mandela's African National Congress, which now rules the country after winning historic all-race elections in 1994.

Kruger, a member of the National Party who has since died, was quoted in the minutes as having told his cabinet colleagues: "The danger is growing black consciousness and the inability to prevent the incidents (protests) because of the military precision with which the students act."
The National Party, which imposed apartheid in 1948 but is now trying to bury its chequered past, said in a statement on Friday it was horrified at the cabinet minutes.

"The cold inhumanity that is reflected in the minutes... fills one with horror. It is a pity that the political situation at the time created a climate that made such thoughts and decisions possible," party secretary-general Roelf Meyer said.
He added that no one who served in the 1976 cabinet was still actively involved in the National Party.

Olivier said current legislation provided for the automatic release of state documents after 30 years, but President Mandela's government had approved the early release of the Kruger minutes after requests from newspapers.
She said outgoing president and National Party leader F.W. de Klerk had sought in vain before losing the 1994 election to have the 30-year period extended an additional 10 years.
Olivier said Archbishop Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission was not affected by the restrictions on release of government papers and had carte blanche to search state archives.
Mandela set up the commission last year to probe human rights abuses during apartheid in the hopes that disclosure and catharsis would help to heal the country's psychological scars.
No cabinet minister from the apartheid era has yet accepted responsibility for specific violations of human rights, though de Klerk has offered a general apology to the truth commission.
